sections.h2: How long someone must occupy land to claim it
sections.html:
Connecticut's limit is fifteen years, and the statute speaks from the owner's side. Section 52-575(a) says no one may enter lands except within fifteen years after the right or title first accrues, or within fifteen years after being ousted from possession. It tells an owner how long the right to take land back lasts and what the owner can do to stop the clock.

A claimant would also have to prove more than time in the house, and an attorney's read of your facts matters more than any short summary. Fifteen years is the number to remember. Nothing in section 52-575 shortens it for an occupant who has been inside only a short while.

sections.h2: How an owner can interrupt the clock
sections.html:
Serve a written notice, record it, then file suit within one year. Under section 52-575(a), entry is not enough on its own. Within the fifteen-year period, a person claiming ownership must give written notice to those in possession saying they dispute the right of possession and want to keep the other party from acquiring it.

The notice must be served and recorded as sections 47-39 and 47-40 provide, and it counts as an interruption of use and possession. The owner must then start a court action within one year after the notice is recorded.

  • Write a notice stating that you dispute the right of possession.
  • Serve it like an original summons, as section 47-39 directs.
  • Record it on the land records in the town where the land lies.
  • Start the court action within one year after recording.

Section 47-39 allows service on a tenant or occupant of the estate for a person outside the state, or failing that, posting a copy on the house or another conspicuous part of the premises. Section 47-40 handles the case of an unknown party. Service rules are technical, so have a lawyer review the paperwork.

sections.h2: Minors, prisoners and people lacking capacity
sections.html:
The time limits stretch a little for them. Under section 52-575(b), someone with a right of entry who was a minor, non compos mentis or imprisoned when the right first accrued, along with that person's heirs, may enter and serve and record notice within five years after reaching full age, regaining sound mind or being released.

This shows up in family houses. A property inherited by an heir who was a child at the owner's death, or a co-owner who spent years incarcerated, may carry a longer window than the fifteen-year headline suggests. The statute also holds that the limit does not begin to run against an owner of a remainder or reversionary interest until the preceding particular estate ends.

So when ownership history is tangled, don't assume the clock ran out on the owner. Pull the chain of title and ask a lawyer to read it.

sections.h2: Someone is living in my house and I never rented to them
sections.html:
Section 47a-23 speaks to this directly. An owner may serve a notice to quit when the premises are occupied by someone who never had a right or privilege to occupy them, and also when someone had that right at first but it has ended.

The notice to quit must be in writing, in the form the statute supplies, and given at least three days before the time stated for the occupant to leave. If the occupant stays, the next step is a summary process case in court. Changing locks or removing belongings is not the next step.

SituationStatute and step
Occupant never had any right to be there47a-23(a)(2), notice to quit
Right to occupy existed but ended47a-23(a)(3), notice to quit
Lease ended or rent not paid47a-23(a)(1), notice to quit
Owner wants to stop an adverse claim running52-575(a), notice served and recorded, suit within one year

A tenant came in under a rental agreement or lease, written or oral. A squatter did not. That split decides which part of section 47a-23 applies. Item (1) covers leases and rental agreements that end by lapse of time, by an expressed stipulation, for violation, or for nonpayment of rent. Items (2) and (3) cover occupants who never had a right or whose right has ended.

Work out which one you have before writing a notice. A person paying rent in cash, or a relative who stayed on after a death, may be treated differently from a stranger who broke in. Text messages, receipts and a written history help. Our Connecticut landlord and tenant page goes into rental occupants in more detail.

Recording a deed is separate from the notice that interrupts an adverse claim. Section 47-10 makes a conveyance ineffective against anyone but the grantor and heirs unless it is recorded in the town where the land lies, so a buyer should always record. The method for interrupting a claim is the recorded notice described in section 52-575(a).

Each of Connecticut's 169 municipalities keeps its own land records. Owners of vacant property can visit regularly and keep dated photographs of its condition and any signs that someone has moved in.

sections.h2: Selling a house with an occupant who will not leave
sections.html:
You can, though it narrows the buyer pool. Anyone needing a mortgage may struggle to close, because possession on closing day is uncertain. Investors who buy as-is sometimes can, but the occupancy will move the price and the timing, and an attorney should read any contract that depends on the occupant leaving.

Before you list, gather what you can: the deed, tax bills, any notice to quit with proof of service, and a note of when you last controlled the property. That file speeds the title search and shows a buyer what is left to do.

sections.h2: Records to keep on vacant or inherited property
sections.html:
Every deadline in this area runs from a date you may later have to prove, so keep a short paper trail. Recording, service and filing each leave a record.

  • The recorded deed, with the town clerk's recording information.
  • Any notice served under section 52-575, with the proof of service and the recording receipt.
  • The date a notice to quit was given under section 47a-23, and the date stated in it.
  • Dated photographs of the property, taken on each visit.
  • Property tax bills, which show who the town treats as owner.

The clerk in the town where the house sits is the right office to ask what is recorded against it.

faqs.q: Can a squatter take ownership of a Connecticut house?
faqs.a: Only if every requirement of adverse possession is met for the full period. Section 52-575 sets a fifteen-year limit on the owner's right to enter, and an attorney should assess the facts.

faqs.q: How many years does adverse possession take in Connecticut?
faqs.a: Fifteen years is the period in section 52-575(a). Longer periods can apply when the owner was a minor, of unsound mind or imprisoned when the right first accrued.

faqs.q: How do I stop someone from claiming my land?
faqs.a: Serve written notice disputing their right of possession, record it as sections 47-39 and 47-40 direct, and begin an action within one year after recording.

faqs.q: What notice do I give someone who never had permission to stay?
faqs.a: A written notice to quit under section 47a-23, given at least three days before the date stated for the occupant to leave. If they stay, a summary process action follows.

faqs.q: Can I sell my house while a squatter is inside?
faqs.a: You can, but financed buyers may struggle to close. An as-is cash buyer may, and the occupancy affects price and timing.
